# Proof

**Setting.** $X$ is a (smooth) manifold of dimension $1$, possibly with boundary; in particular $X$ is Hausdorff and every point $x\in X$ has arbitrarily small open neighbourhoods $U$ with a homeomorphism $\varphi:U\to I$ where $\varphi(x)=0$ and $I=(-1,1)$ (interior point) or $I=[0,1)$ (boundary point). [Given an open $W\ni x$, take any chart $\varphi_0:U_0\to\mathbb R$ or $[0,\infty)$ at $x$; $\varphi_0(U_0\cap W)$ is a (relatively) open set containing $\varphi_0(x)$, so it contains $(\varphi_0(x)-r,\varphi_0(x)+r)$, resp. $[0,r)$ if $\varphi_0(x)=0$ is a boundary value, for some $r>0$; restrict and apply an affine map.] $L\subseteq X$ carries the subspace topology, and a diffeomorphism from an open interval onto $L$ is in particular a homeomorphism. Composing with a homeomorphism $(0,1)\to(a,b)$, we get a continuous injective map $g:(0,1)\to X$ with $g((0,1))=L$ that is a homeomorphism onto $L$. Only continuity and injectivity of $g$ will be used.

**Step 1 (points of $\overline L\setminus L$ are "end limits").** Put
$$A=\bigcap_{0<\varepsilon<1}\overline{g((0,\varepsilon))},\qquad B=\bigcap_{0<\varepsilon<1}\overline{g((1-\varepsilon,1))}.$$
Claim: $\overline L\setminus L\subseteq A\cup B$.
Let $p\in\overline L\setminus L$. For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$,
$L=g((0,\varepsilon))\cup g([\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon])\cup g((1-\varepsilon,1))$. The middle set is compact (continuous image of a compact set), hence closed in the Hausdorff space $X$, and does not contain $p$. Since the closure of a finite union is the union of the closures, $p\in\overline{g((0,\varepsilon))}\cup\overline{g((1-\varepsilon,1))}$ for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$.
Suppose $p\notin A$. The sets $\overline{g((0,\varepsilon))}$ increase with $\varepsilon$, so there is $\varepsilon_0\in(0,1/2)$ with $p\notin\overline{g((0,\varepsilon))}$ for all $\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$. Hence $p\in\overline{g((1-\varepsilon,1))}$ for all $\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, and since these sets also increase with $\varepsilon$, for all $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$. So $p\in B$.

**Step 2 ($A\setminus L$ has at most one point).** Suppose $p\in A\setminus L$ and $q\in A$ with $q\neq p$. By Hausdorffness choose disjoint open sets $W\ni p$, $W'\ni q$. Choose an open neighbourhood $U\subseteq W$ of $p$ and a homeomorphism $\varphi:U\to I$ with $\varphi(p)=0$, $I=(-1,1)$ or $I=[0,1)$. Then $U\cap W'=\emptyset$. Let $O=g^{-1}(U)$, an open subset of $(0,1)$.

Since $q\in\overline{g((0,1/2))}$ and $W'$ is an open neighbourhood of $q$, there is $s_1\in(0,1/2)$ with $g(s_1)\in W'$. Since $p\in\overline{g((0,s_1))}$, there is $t\in(0,s_1)$ with $g(t)\in U$. Since $q\in\overline{g((0,t))}$, there is $s_2\in(0,t)$ with $g(s_2)\in W'$. Thus $s_2<t<s_1$, $t\in O$, and $s_1,s_2\notin O$ (as $W'\cap U=\emptyset$).

Let $C$ be the connected component of $O$ containing $t$. Components of an open subset of $\mathbb R$ are open intervals, so $C=(\alpha,\beta)$, and since $s_1,s_2\notin O$ we have $s_2\le\alpha<t<\beta\le s_1$; in particular $0<\alpha<\beta<1$, and $\alpha,\beta\notin O$ (an endpoint of a component of an open set is not in the set, otherwise the component could be enlarged).

The map $h=\varphi\circ g|_C:C\to I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is continuous and injective on the interval $C$, hence strictly monotone (standard consequence of the intermediate value theorem), and its image $J=h(C)$ is an interval with no least or greatest element (a strictly monotone map on an open interval attains no extreme value), i.e. $J=(c,d)$ with $c<d$, and $J\subseteq I\subseteq[-1,1]$, so $c,d$ are finite. As $t\to\alpha^+$, $h(t)$ converges to one of $c,d$ (monotone limit), call it $x$.

*Claim: $x\notin I$.* Otherwise $g(t)=\varphi^{-1}(h(t))\to\varphi^{-1}(x)$ in $U$, hence in $X$, as $t\to\alpha^+$ (continuity of $\varphi^{-1}$, and $U$ has the subspace topology). But also $g(t)\to g(\alpha)$ by continuity of $g$ at $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Limits in a Hausdorff space are unique, so $g(\alpha)=\varphi^{-1}(x)\in U$, i.e. $\alpha\in O$, a contradiction.
In the same way, the limit of $h(t)$ as $t\to\beta^-$, which is the other one of $c,d$, is not in $I$. So $c,d\notin I$.

If $I=(-1,1)$: $c,d\in[-1,1]\setminus(-1,1)$ with $c<d$ force $c=-1$, $d=1$, so $J=I\ni0=\varphi(p)$. Then $p=g(u)$ for some $u\in C$, so $p\in L$, a contradiction.
If $I=[0,1)$: $c,d\in[0,1]\setminus[0,1)=\{1\}$, contradicting $c<d$.

Hence no such $q$ exists: if $A\setminus L\neq\emptyset$ then $A$ (and so $A\setminus L$) is a single point. So $|A\setminus L|\le1$.

**Step 3.** Applying Step 2 to $\tilde g(t)=g(1-t)$ (also continuous, injective, with image $L$, and whose set "$A$" is $B$) gives $|B\setminus L|\le1$.

**Conclusion.** By Step 1, $\overline L\setminus L\subseteq(A\setminus L)\cup(B\setminus L)$, which has at most two points. $\blacksquare$
